# cynic 3.13.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cynic/3.13.2

# Overview

Cynic is a GraphQL library for Rust. It's not the first but it takes a different approach from the existing libraries.

Existing libraries take a query first approach to GQL - you write a query using GraphQL and libraries use that to generate Rust structs for you using macros. This is really easy and great for getting going quickly. However, if you want to use structs that aren't quite what the macros output you're out of luck. Some more complex use cases like sharing structs among queries are also commonly not supported.

Cynic takes a different approach - it uses Rust structs to define queries and
generates GraphQL from them. This gives you freedom to control the structs
you'll be working with while still enjoying type safe queries, checked against
the GraphQL schema. When its built in `derives` don't do exactly what you
want it provides lower level APIs to hook in and fetch the data you want in the
format you want to work with it.

Of course writing out all the structs to represent a large GraphQL query can be
quite challenging, and GraphQL has excellent tooling for building queries
usually. Cynic provides [ querygen](https://generator.cynic-rs.dev) to help with this - you write a
GraphQL query using the existing GQL tooling and it'll generate some cynic
structs to make that query. You can use this as a starting point for your
projects - either adding on to the rust structs directly, or re-using

`querygen` as appropriate.### Features

Cynic is currently a work in progress, but the following features are supported:

- Typesafe queries & mutations.
- Defining custom scalars.
- Building dynamic (but still type checked) queries at run time.
- Query arguments including input objects
- Interfaces & union types
- Introspection via `cynic-cli``cynic-introspection`
- GraphQL Subscriptions via `graphql-ws-client`
- Field directives (`@skip`,`@include`and any custom directives that don't require client support)

### Documentation

Cynic is documented in a few places:

- There's a guide to using cynic on [cynic-rs.dev](https://cynic-rs.dev)
- The reference documentation on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/cynic)

### Inspiration

- [graphql-client](https://github.com/graphql-rust/graphql-client), the original Rust GraphQL client. This is a great library for using GraphQL from Rust. It wasn't quite what I wanted but it might be what you want.
- The idea of encoding the GraphQL typesystem into a DSL was taken from
[elm-graphql](https://github.com/dillonkearns/elm-graphql).
- Most of the JSON decoding APIs were taken from [Json.Decode in Elm](https://package.elm-lang.org/packages/elm/json/latest/Json.Decode).
- Deriving code from structs is a fairly common Rust pattern, though [serde](https://serde.rs)in particular provided inspiration for the derive APIs.

### Getting Help

If you want help with cynic you can join the #cynic chat room on IRC using any of these options:

- [A Web UI](https://web.libera.chat/#cynic)
- [Using this link if you have an IRC client](ircs://irc.libera.chat:6697/#cynic)
- [Selecting a client from joinrc.at](https://joinirc.at/ircs://irc.libera.chat:6697/#cynic)
- Joining #cynic on irc.libera.chat if you know what you're doing

# cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cynic/3.13.2/target-redirect/aarch64-apple-darwin/cynic/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cynic)Cynic

Cynic is a GraphQL query builder & data mapper for Rust.

This documentation is primarily intended to be a reference for specific
functions, for a guide to using `Cynic` see the website: [cynic-rs.dev](https://cynic-rs.dev).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

To get started with Cynic you’ll need a GraphQL schema for the API you wish to query. The examples will be using the star wars API.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-a-query-dsl)Generating a Query DSL

Once you’ve got your schema installed locally, you’ll need to use the
`use_schema` macro to generate a schema module:

```
mod schema {
    cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql");
}
```
This macro generates a few things:

- Some structs to represent the Input types the underlying schema. You may need to use these to build mutations or as parameters to queries.
- Definitions of all the Enums in the provided schema. You’ll need these if you want to use any enum types.
- Type safe selection set functions.  These can be used to build up a query
manually, though it’s usually easier to use the `QueryFragment`derive functionality explained below. Hopefully you’ll not need to use these directly too often.

Though using macros to generate these is convenient, it does leave a lot of
code to the imagination.  You can get a glimpse of the things this defines
by running `cargo doc --document-private-items` and having a look in the
`schema` module. It’s not ideal, but at least provides some visibility into
the various enum types.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-queryfragments)Creating QueryFragments

Now that you have a schema defined, you can start building some queries.
Cynic lets you do this by deriving `QueryFragment` for a struct.  For
example, if we wanted to know what director title & director a Star Wars
film had, we could define this `QueryFragment`:

```
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql")]
struct Film {
    title: Option<String>,
    director: Option<String>,
}
// This `Film` struct can now be used as the type of a field on any other
// `QueryFragment` struct and cynic will know how to turn that into a GraphQL
// query, and populate the `Film` struct from the response.
// For example, if we wanted to know the Director for a particular film:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQuery {
    // Here we use the `#[arguments()]` attribute on the `film` field to provide a
    // hard coded film ID to look up.  Though useful for demonstration, hard coded
    // arguments like this aren't much use in reality.  For more details on providing
    // runtime arguments please see below.
    #[arguments(id = cynic::Id::new("ZmlsbXM6MQ=="))]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// You can then build a `cynic::Operation` from this fragment
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
```
`operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
`cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
`cynic::Operation`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
                    .post("a_url")
                    .json(&operation)
                    .send()?;
let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
```
After this code has run, result will be an instance of
`GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#dynamic-query-arguments)Dynamic Query Arguments

The query above was useful for demonstration, but you’ll usually want to be able to provide parameters to your query. To do this, you should define a struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:

```
// Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
// `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
#[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
struct FilmArguments {
    id: Option<cynic::Id>,
}
// You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
// `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root",
    // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
    // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
    variables = "FilmArguments"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
    // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
    #[arguments(id: $id)]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// Then we can build a query using this new struct;
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs::build(FilmArguments {
    id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.

- `http-surf`adds integration with the- `surf`
- `http-reqwest`adds async integration with the- `reqwest`
- `http-reqwest-blocking`adds blocking integration with the- `reqwest`
- `rkyv`can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.

It’s worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly
if you’re targeting WASM.  In particular the `url` crate has
[known issues](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/557) when
targeting web assembly.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_coercions.html)- coercions
- Implements the default GraphQL list & option coercion rules for a type.
- [impl_](https://docs.rs/macro.impl_scalar.html)- scalar
- Implements a set of scalar traits for the given type & type lock.
- [use_](https://docs.rs/macro.use_schema.html)- schema
- Imports a schema for use by cynic.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphQlError.html)- QlError
- A model describing an error which has taken place during execution.
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphQlErrorLocation.html)- QlError - Location
- A line and column offset describing the location of an error within a GraphQL document.
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphQlResponse.html)- QlResponse
- The response to a GraphQl operation
- [Id](https://docs.rs/struct.Id.html)
- A GraphQL `ID`
- [Operation](https://docs.rs/struct.Operation.html)
- An Operation that can be sent to a remote GraphQL server.
- [Operation](https://docs.rs/struct.OperationBuilder.html)- Builder
- Low level builder for [Operation](https://docs.rs/struct.Operation.html).
- [Streaming](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamingOperation.html)- Operation
- A StreamingOperation is an Operation that expects a stream of results.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- A segment of a GraphQL error path.
- [Operation](https://docs.rs/enum.OperationBuildError.html)- Build - Error
- Errors that can occur when building the operation

- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.Enum.html)
- A GraphQL Enum.
- [Inline](https://docs.rs/trait.InlineFragments.html)- Fragments
- A QueryFragment that contains a set of inline fragments
- [Input](https://docs.rs/trait.InputObject.html)- Object
- A GraphQL input object.
- [Mutation](https://docs.rs/trait.MutationBuilder.html)- Builder
- Provides a `build`function on`QueryFragment`s that represent a mutation
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.QueryBuilder.html)- Builder
- Provides a `build`function on`QueryFragment`s that represent a query
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.QueryFragment.html)- Fragment
- A trait that marks a type as part of a GraphQL query.
- [Subscription](https://docs.rs/trait.SubscriptionBuilder.html)- Builder
- Provides a `build`function on`QueryFragment`s that represent a subscription

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [schema](https://docs.rs/attr.schema.html)
- Imports a registered schema into a schema module.
- [schema_](https://docs.rs/attr.schema_for_derives.html)- for_ - derives
- An attribute macro to automatically add schema attributes to cynic derives.

use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
```
`operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
`cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
`cynic::Operation`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
                    .post("a_url")
                    .json(&operation)
                    .send()?;
let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
```
After this code has run, result will be an instance of
`GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#dynamic-query-arguments)Dynamic Query Arguments

The query above was useful for demonstration, but you’ll usually want to be able to provide parameters to your query. To do this, you should define a struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:

```
// Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
// `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
#[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
struct FilmArguments {
    id: Option<cynic::Id>,
}
// You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
// `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root",
    // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
    // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
    variables = "FilmArguments"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
    // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
    #[arguments(id: $id)]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// Then we can build a query using this new struct;
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs::build(FilmArguments {
    id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.

- `http-surf`adds integration with the- `surf`
- `http-reqwest`adds async integration with the- `reqwest`
- `http-reqwest-blocking`adds blocking integration with the- `reqwest`
- `rkyv`can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.

It’s worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly
if you’re targeting WASM.  In particular the `url` crate has
[known issues](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/557) when
targeting web assembly.

# cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cynic/3.13.2/target-redirect/cynic/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cynic)Cynic

Cynic is a GraphQL query builder & data mapper for Rust.

This documentation is primarily intended to be a reference for specific
functions, for a guide to using `Cynic` see the website: [cynic-rs.dev](https://cynic-rs.dev).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

To get started with Cynic you’ll need a GraphQL schema for the API you wish to query. The examples will be using the star wars API.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-a-query-dsl)Generating a Query DSL

Once you’ve got your schema installed locally, you’ll need to use the
`use_schema` macro to generate a schema module:

```
mod schema {
    cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql");
}
```
This macro generates a few things:

- Some structs to represent the Input types the underlying schema. You may need to use these to build mutations or as parameters to queries.
- Definitions of all the Enums in the provided schema. You’ll need these if you want to use any enum types.
- Type safe selection set functions.  These can be used to build up a query
manually, though it’s usually easier to use the `QueryFragment`derive functionality explained below. Hopefully you’ll not need to use these directly too often.

Though using macros to generate these is convenient, it does leave a lot of
code to the imagination.  You can get a glimpse of the things this defines
by running `cargo doc --document-private-items` and having a look in the
`schema` module. It’s not ideal, but at least provides some visibility into
the various enum types.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-queryfragments)Creating QueryFragments

Now that you have a schema defined, you can start building some queries.
Cynic lets you do this by deriving `QueryFragment` for a struct.  For
example, if we wanted to know what director title & director a Star Wars
film had, we could define this `QueryFragment`:

```
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql")]
struct Film {
    title: Option<String>,
    director: Option<String>,
}
// This `Film` struct can now be used as the type of a field on any other
// `QueryFragment` struct and cynic will know how to turn that into a GraphQL
// query, and populate the `Film` struct from the response.
// For example, if we wanted to know the Director for a particular film:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQuery {
    // Here we use the `#[arguments()]` attribute on the `film` field to provide a
    // hard coded film ID to look up.  Though useful for demonstration, hard coded
    // arguments like this aren't much use in reality.  For more details on providing
    // runtime arguments please see below.
    #[arguments(id = cynic::Id::new("ZmlsbXM6MQ=="))]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// You can then build a `cynic::Operation` from this fragment
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
```
`operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
`cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
`cynic::Operation`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
                    .post("a_url")
                    .json(&operation)
                    .send()?;
let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
```
After this code has run, result will be an instance of
`GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#dynamic-query-arguments)Dynamic Query Arguments

The query above was useful for demonstration, but you’ll usually want to be able to provide parameters to your query. To do this, you should define a struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:

```
// Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
// `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
#[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
struct FilmArguments {
    id: Option<cynic::Id>,
}
// You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
// `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root",
    // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
    // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
    variables = "FilmArguments"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
    // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
    #[arguments(id: $id)]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// Then we can build a query using this new struct;
use cynic::QueryBuilder;

    id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.

- `http-surf`adds integration with the- `surf`
- `http-reqwest`adds async integration with the- `reqwest`
- `http-reqwest-blocking`adds blocking integration with the- `reqwest`
- `rkyv`can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.

It’s worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly

[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! #[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! #[cynic(schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql")]
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! struct Film {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!     title: Option<String>,
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     director: Option<String>,
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! }
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! // This `Film` struct can now be used as the type of a field on any other
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! // `QueryFragment` struct and cynic will know how to turn that into a GraphQL
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! // query, and populate the `Film` struct from the response.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! // For example, if we wanted to know the Director for a particular film:
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! #[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! #[cynic(
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!     schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!     graphql_type = "Root"
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! )]
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! struct FilmDirectorQuery {
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!     // Here we use the `#[arguments()]` attribute on the `film` field to provide a
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!     // hard coded film ID to look up.  Though useful for demonstration, hard coded
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!     // arguments like this aren't much use in reality.  For more details on providing
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     // runtime arguments please see below.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!     #[arguments(id = cynic::Id::new("ZmlsbXM6MQ=="))]
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     film: Option<Film>,
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! }
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! // You can then build a `cynic::Operation` from this fragment
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! use cynic::QueryBuilder;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ```
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! `operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! `cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! `cynic::Operation`
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ```rust,ignore
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!                     .post("a_url")
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!                     .json(&operation)
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!                     .send()?;
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! ```
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! After this code has run, result will be an instance of
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! `GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ### Dynamic Query Arguments
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! The query above was useful for demonstration, but you'll usually want to be
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! able to provide parameters to your query.  To do this, you should define a
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! ```rust
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! # mod schema {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! #   cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql");
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! # }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! # #[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! # #[cynic(
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! #    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! # )]
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! # struct Film {
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! #    title: Option<String>,
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! #    director: Option<String>
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! # }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! // Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! // `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! #[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! struct FilmArguments {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     id: Option<cynic::Id>,
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! // You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! // `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! #[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! #[cynic(
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!     schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     graphql_type = "Root",
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     variables = "FilmArguments"
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! )]
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!     // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!     #[arguments(id: $id)]
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!     film: Option<Film>,
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! }
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! // Then we can build a query using this new struct;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! use cynic::QueryBuilder;
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! let operation = FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs::build(FilmArguments {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!     id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! });
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! ```
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! ## Feature Flags
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! - `http-surf` adds integration with the [`surf`](https://github.com/http-rs/surf)
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!   http client.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! - `http-reqwest` adds async integration with the [`reqwest`](https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest)
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!   http client.
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! - `http-reqwest-blocking` adds blocking integration with the [`reqwest`](https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!   http client.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! - `rkyv` can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! It's worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! if you're targeting WASM.  In particular the `url` crate has
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! [known issues](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/557) when
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! targeting web assembly.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)

[210](https://docs.rs#210)/// Implements a set of scalar traits for the given type & type lock.
[211](https://docs.rs#211)///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)/// For example, to use `uuid::Uuid` for a `Uuid` type defined in a schema:
[213](https://docs.rs#213)///
[214](https://docs.rs#214)/// ```rust
[215](https://docs.rs#215)/// # #[macro_use] extern crate cynic;
[216](https://docs.rs#216)/// # // Faking the uuid module here because it's easier than
[217](https://docs.rs#217)/// # // actually pulling it in
[218](https://docs.rs#218)/// #
[219](https://docs.rs#219)/// # mod schema { cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/test_cases.graphql"); }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)/// # mod uuid { pub struct Uuid(String); }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)/// impl_scalar!(uuid::Uuid, schema::UUID);
[222](https://docs.rs#222)/// ```
[223](https://docs.rs#223)///
[224](https://docs.rs#224)/// This macro can be used on any type that implements `serde::Serialize`,
[225](https://docs.rs#225)/// provided the `schema` is defined in the current crate
[226](https://docs.rs#226)#[macro_export]
[227](https://docs.rs#227)macro_rules! impl_scalar {
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    ($type:path, $type_lock:ident) => {
[229](https://docs.rs#229)        $crate::impl_scalar!($type, $type_lock, self);
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    };
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ($type:path, $type_lock_segment:ident $(:: $type_lock_rest :ident)::+) => {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        $crate::impl_scalar!($type, $($type_lock_rest)::*, $type_lock_segment);
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    };
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    ($type:path, $type_lock_segment:ident $(:: $type_lock_rest :ident)::+, $schema_module:ident $(:: $schema_module_rest : ident)*) => {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        $crate::impl_scalar!($type, $($type_lock_rest)::*, $schema_module(::$schema_module_rest)*::$type_lock_segment)
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    };
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    ($type:path, $type_lock:ident, $schema_module:ident $(:: $schema_module_rest : ident)*) => {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        #[automatically_derived]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)        impl $crate::schema::IsScalar<$schema_module$(::$schema_module_rest)*::$type_lock> for $type {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)            type SchemaType = $schema_module$(::$schema_module_rest)*::$type_lock;
[241](https://docs.rs#241)        }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        // We derive a simple CoercesTo here, but since we don't own $type we can't
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        // impl any of the more advanced coercions.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)        #[automatically_derived]
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        impl $crate::coercions::CoercesTo<$schema_module$(::$schema_module_rest)*::$type_lock> for $type {}
[247](https://docs.rs#247)
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        #[automatically_derived]
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        impl $schema_module$(::$schema_module_rest)*::variable::Variable for $type {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            const TYPE: cynic::variables::VariableType = cynic::variables::VariableType::Named(
[251](https://docs.rs#251)                <$schema_module$(::$schema_module_rest)*::$type_lock as $crate::schema::NamedType>::NAME,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            );
[253](https://docs.rs#253)        }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    };
[255](https://docs.rs#255)}
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)#[macro_export(local_inner_macros)]
[258](https://docs.rs#258)#[doc(hidden)]
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// Asserts that the type implements _all_ of the given traits.
[260](https://docs.rs#260)macro_rules! assert_impl {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    ($type:ty [$($impl_generics: tt)*] [$($where_clause: tt)*]: $($trait:path),+ $(,)?) => {
[262](https://docs.rs#262)        const _: () = {
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            // Only callable when `$type` implements all traits in `$($trait)+`.
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            fn assert_impl_all<T: ?Sized $(+ $trait)+>() {}
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            fn do_assert $($impl_generics)* () $($where_clause)* {
[266](https://docs.rs#266)                assert_impl_all::<$type>();
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            }
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        };
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    };

# cynic::schema - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cynic/3.13.2/cynic/schema/index.html

## Expand description

Traits for describing a GraphQL schema in Rust.

The `use_schema` macro will mostly output types that make use of the
traits in this module to describe the schema.  The derives then combine
these types with the `QueryBuilder` type to enforce the restrictions
of the schema.

Note that this module is mostly concerned with the marker types output
by `use_schema`, *not* the actual types users work with.  The traits
will usually be implemented on marker types, the geneirc parameters will
usually be marker types and the associated types will also usually be
markers.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Field](https://docs.rs/trait.Field.html)
- Indicates that a struct represents a Field in a graphql schema.
- [Field](https://docs.rs/trait.FieldDirective.html)- Directive
- Indicates that a type represents a GraphQL directive that can be used in field position.
- [HasArgument](https://docs.rs/trait.HasArgument.html)
- Indicates that a field has an argument
- [HasField](https://docs.rs/trait.HasField.html)
- Indicates that a type has a given field
- [HasInput](https://docs.rs/trait.HasInputField.html)- Field
- Indicates that an input object has a given field
- [HasSubtype](https://docs.rs/trait.HasSubtype.html)
- Indicates that a type has a subtype relationship with another type
- [Input](https://docs.rs/trait.InputObjectMarker.html)- Object - Marker
- Indicates that a type is an `InputObject`
- [IsScalar](https://docs.rs/trait.IsScalar.html)
- Indicates that a type is a scalar that maps to the given schema scalar.
- [Mutation](https://docs.rs/trait.MutationRoot.html)- Root
- A marker trait that indicates a particular type is at the root of a GraphQL schemas mutation hierarchy.
- [Named](https://docs.rs/trait.NamedType.html)- Type
- A marker type with a name.
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.QueryRoot.html)- Root
- A marker trait that indicates a particular type is at the root of a GraphQL schemas query hierarchy.
- [Subscription](https://docs.rs/trait.SubscriptionRoot.html)- Root
- A marker trait that indicates a particular type is at the root of a GraphQL schemas subscription hierarchy.

# impl_scalar in cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cynic/3.13.2/cynic/macro.impl_scalar.html

```
macro_rules! impl_scalar {
    ($type:path, $type_lock:ident) => { ... };
    ($type:path, $type_lock_segment:ident $(:: $type_lock_rest :ident)::+) => { ... };
    ($type:path, $type_lock_segment:ident $(:: $type_lock_rest :ident)::+, $schema_module:ident $(:: $schema_module_rest : ident)*) => { ... };
    ($type:path, $type_lock:ident, $schema_module:ident $(:: $schema_module_rest : ident)*) => { ... };

```
## Expand description

Implements a set of scalar traits for the given type & type lock.

For example, to use `uuid::Uuid` for a `Uuid` type defined in a schema:

`impl_scalar!(uuid::Uuid, schema::UUID);`This macro can be used on any type that implements `serde::Serialize`,
provided the `schema` is defined in the current crate

# Id in cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cynic/3.13.2/cynic/struct.Id.html

`pub struct Id(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A GraphQL `ID`

Any field in a GraphQL schema that has the type `ID` should be represented
by this struct.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Constructs an `ID` from a `String`, `&str` or similar

`cynic::Id::new("123");`Converts a reference to a String to a reference to an Id

To be used when you can access an `&String` which you want to assume is
an `Id` for use in Cynic structures without reallocating

If you don’t have a `String` at hand but only an `&str`, you should know
that these can be used directly in `InputObject`s as well when the
target GraphQL type is an `Id`.

# cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cynic/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/cynic/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cynic)Cynic

Cynic is a GraphQL query builder & data mapper for Rust.

This documentation is primarily intended to be a reference for specific
functions, for a guide to using `Cynic` see the website: [cynic-rs.dev](https://cynic-rs.dev).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

To get started with Cynic you’ll need a GraphQL schema for the API you wish to query. The examples will be using the star wars API.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-a-query-dsl)Generating a Query DSL

Once you’ve got your schema installed locally, you’ll need to use the
`use_schema` macro to generate a schema module:

```
mod schema {
    cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql");
}
```
This macro generates a few things:

- Some structs to represent the Input types the underlying schema. You may need to use these to build mutations or as parameters to queries.
- Definitions of all the Enums in the provided schema. You’ll need these if you want to use any enum types.
- Type safe selection set functions.  These can be used to build up a query
manually, though it’s usually easier to use the `QueryFragment`derive functionality explained below. Hopefully you’ll not need to use these directly too often.

Though using macros to generate these is convenient, it does leave a lot of
code to the imagination.  You can get a glimpse of the things this defines
by running `cargo doc --document-private-items` and having a look in the
`schema` module. It’s not ideal, but at least provides some visibility into
the various enum types.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-queryfragments)Creating QueryFragments

Now that you have a schema defined, you can start building some queries.
Cynic lets you do this by deriving `QueryFragment` for a struct.  For
example, if we wanted to know what director title & director a Star Wars
film had, we could define this `QueryFragment`:

```
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql")]
struct Film {
    title: Option<String>,
    director: Option<String>,
}
// This `Film` struct can now be used as the type of a field on any other
// `QueryFragment` struct and cynic will know how to turn that into a GraphQL
// query, and populate the `Film` struct from the response.
// For example, if we wanted to know the Director for a particular film:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQuery {
    // Here we use the `#[arguments()]` attribute on the `film` field to provide a
    // hard coded film ID to look up.  Though useful for demonstration, hard coded
    // arguments like this aren't much use in reality.  For more details on providing
    // runtime arguments please see below.
    #[arguments(id = cynic::Id::new("ZmlsbXM6MQ=="))]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// You can then build a `cynic::Operation` from this fragment
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
```
`operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
`cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
`cynic::Operation`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
                    .post("a_url")
                    .json(&operation)
                    .send()?;
let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
```
After this code has run, result will be an instance of
`GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#dynamic-query-arguments)Dynamic Query Arguments

The query above was useful for demonstration, but you’ll usually want to be able to provide parameters to your query. To do this, you should define a struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:

```
// Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
// `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
#[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
struct FilmArguments {
    id: Option<cynic::Id>,
}
// You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
// `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root",
    // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
    // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
    variables = "FilmArguments"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
    // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
    #[arguments(id: $id)]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// Then we can build a query using this new struct;
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs::build(FilmArguments {
    id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.

- `http-surf`adds integration with the- `surf`
- `http-reqwest`adds async integration with the- `reqwest`
- `http-reqwest-blocking`adds blocking integration with the- `reqwest`
- `rkyv`can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.

It’s worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly
if you’re targeting WASM.  In particular the `url` crate has
[known issues](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/557) when
targeting web assembly.

# cynic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cynic/latest/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/cynic/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#cynic)Cynic

Cynic is a GraphQL query builder & data mapper for Rust.

This documentation is primarily intended to be a reference for specific
functions, for a guide to using `Cynic` see the website: [cynic-rs.dev](https://cynic-rs.dev).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

To get started with Cynic you’ll need a GraphQL schema for the API you wish to query. The examples will be using the star wars API.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-a-query-dsl)Generating a Query DSL

Once you’ve got your schema installed locally, you’ll need to use the
`use_schema` macro to generate a schema module:

```
mod schema {
    cynic::use_schema!("../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql");
}
```
This macro generates a few things:

- Some structs to represent the Input types the underlying schema. You may need to use these to build mutations or as parameters to queries.
- Definitions of all the Enums in the provided schema. You’ll need these if you want to use any enum types.
- Type safe selection set functions.  These can be used to build up a query
manually, though it’s usually easier to use the `QueryFragment`derive functionality explained below. Hopefully you’ll not need to use these directly too often.

Though using macros to generate these is convenient, it does leave a lot of
code to the imagination.  You can get a glimpse of the things this defines
by running `cargo doc --document-private-items` and having a look in the
`schema` module. It’s not ideal, but at least provides some visibility into
the various enum types.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-queryfragments)Creating QueryFragments

Now that you have a schema defined, you can start building some queries.
Cynic lets you do this by deriving `QueryFragment` for a struct.  For
example, if we wanted to know what director title & director a Star Wars
film had, we could define this `QueryFragment`:

```
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql")]
struct Film {
    title: Option<String>,
    director: Option<String>,
}
// This `Film` struct can now be used as the type of a field on any other
// `QueryFragment` struct and cynic will know how to turn that into a GraphQL
// query, and populate the `Film` struct from the response.
// For example, if we wanted to know the Director for a particular film:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQuery {
    // Here we use the `#[arguments()]` attribute on the `film` field to provide a
    // hard coded film ID to look up.  Though useful for demonstration, hard coded
    // arguments like this aren't much use in reality.  For more details on providing
    // runtime arguments please see below.
    #[arguments(id = cynic::Id::new("ZmlsbXM6MQ=="))]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// You can then build a `cynic::Operation` from this fragment
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQuery::build(());
```
`operation` above implements `serde::Serialize` so can be used with any HTTP
client.  A selection of HTTP client integrations are provided in
`cynic::http` - see the docs there for examples of using a
`cynic::Operation`

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let response = reqwest::blocking::Client::new()
                    .post("a_url")
                    .json(&operation)
                    .send()?;
let result = response.json::<GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>>()?;
```
After this code has run, result will be an instance of
`GraphQlResponse<FilmDirectorQuery>` with the film populated appropriately.

[§](https://docs.rs#dynamic-query-arguments)Dynamic Query Arguments

The query above was useful for demonstration, but you’ll usually want to be able to provide parameters to your query. To do this, you should define a struct that contains all of the parameters you want to provide:

```
// Deriving `QueryVariables` allows this struct to be used as variables in a
// `QueryFragment`, whether it represents part of a query or a whole query.
#[derive(cynic::QueryVariables)]
struct FilmArguments {
    id: Option<cynic::Id>,
}
// You can now define a query to use these arguments on.  For example, to make
// `FilmDirectorQuery` a bit more dynamic:
#[derive(cynic::QueryFragment)]
#[cynic(
    schema_path = "../schemas/starwars.schema.graphql",
    graphql_type = "Root",
    // By adding the `variables` parameter to our `QueryFragment` we've made a variable
    // named `args` available for use in the `arguments` attribute.
    variables = "FilmArguments"
)]
struct FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs {
    // Here we use `args`, which we've declared above to be an instance of `FilmArguments`
    #[arguments(id: $id)]
    film: Option<Film>,
}
// Then we can build a query using this new struct;
use cynic::QueryBuilder;
let operation = FilmDirectorQueryWithArgs::build(FilmArguments {
    id: Some("ZmlsbXM6MQ==".into()),
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

Cynic has a few features that are controlled by feature flags.

- `http-surf`adds integration with the- `surf`
- `http-reqwest`adds async integration with the- `reqwest`
- `http-reqwest-blocking`adds blocking integration with the- `reqwest`
- `rkyv`can be used to speed up compiles when working with large schemas.

It’s worth noting that each of these features pulls in extra
dependencies, which may impact your build size.  Particularly
if you’re targeting WASM.  In particular the `url` crate has
[known issues](https://github.com/servo/rust-url/issues/557) when
targeting web assembly.

# cynic 3.13.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cynic/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# cynic 3.13.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/cynic/latest/source/README.md

```

Cynic is a GraphQL library for Rust. It's not the first but it takes a
different approach from the existing libraries.
Existing libraries take a query first approach to GQL - you write a query using
GraphQL and libraries use that to generate Rust structs for you using macros.
This is really easy and great for getting going quickly. However, if you want
to use structs that aren't quite what the macros output you're out of luck.
Some more complex use cases like sharing structs among queries are also
commonly not supported.
Cynic takes a different approach - it uses Rust structs to define queries and
generates GraphQL from them. This gives you freedom to control the structs
you'll be working with while still enjoying type safe queries, checked against
the GraphQL schema. When its built in `derives` don't do exactly what you
want it provides lower level APIs to hook in and fetch the data you want in the
format you want to work with it.
Of course writing out all the structs to represent a large GraphQL query can be
quite challenging, and GraphQL has excellent tooling for building queries
usually. Cynic provides [`querygen`][1] to help with this - you write a
GraphQL query using the existing GQL tooling and it'll generate some cynic
structs to make that query. You can use this as a starting point for your
projects - either adding on to the rust structs directly, or re-using
`querygen` as appropriate.
Cynic is currently a work in progress, but the following features are
supported:
- -------
Cynic is documented in a few places:
1. 2.
- ---
If you want help with cynic you can join the #cynic chat room on
IRC using any of these options:
- ---
```

# darling - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/darling/^0.20/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#darling)Darling

Darling is a tool for declarative attribute parsing in proc macro implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Darling takes considerable design inspiration from [ serde](https://serde.rs). A data structure that can be
read from any attribute implements

`FromMeta` (or has an implementation automatically
generated using `derive`). Any crate can provide `FromMeta` implementations, even one not
specifically geared towards proc-macro authors.Proc-macro crates should provide their own structs which implement or derive `FromDeriveInput`,
`FromField`, `FromVariant`, `FromGenerics`, *et alia* to gather settings relevant to their operation.

[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)Attributes

There are a number of attributes that `darling` exposes to enable finer-grained control over the code
it generates.

- **Field renaming**: You can use- `#[darling(rename="new_name")]`on a field to change the name Darling looks for. You can also use- `#[darling(rename_all="...")]`at the struct or enum level to apply a casing rule to all fields or variants.
- **Map function**: You can use- `#[darling(map="path::to::function")]`to run code on a field before its stored in the struct.
- **Default values**: You can use- `#[darling(default)]`at the type or field level to use that type’s default value to fill in values not specified by the caller.
- **Skipped fields**: You can skip a variant or field using- `#[darling(skip)]`. Fields marked with this will fall back to- `Default::default()`for their value, but you can override that with an explicit default or a value from the type-level default.
- **Custom shorthand**: Use- `#[darling(from_word = ...)]`on a struct or enum to override how a simple word is interpreted. By default, it is an error for your macro’s user to fail to specify the fields of your struct, but with this you can choose to instead produce a set of default values. This takes either a path or a closure whose signature matches- `FromMeta::from_word`.
- **Custom handling for missing fields**: When a field is not present and- `#[darling(default)]`is not used, derived impls will call- `FromMeta::from_none`on that field’s type to try and get the fallback value for the field. Usually, there is not a fallback value, so a missing field error is generated.- `Option<T: FromMeta>`uses this to make options optional without requiring- `#[darling(default)]`declarations, and structs and enums can use this themselves with- `#[darling(from_none = ...)]`. This takes either a path or a closure whose signature matches- `FromMeta::from_none`.

[§](https://docs.rs#forwarded-fields)Forwarded Fields

All derivable traits except `FromMeta` support forwarding some fields from the input AST to the derived struct.
These fields are matched up by identifier **before** `rename` attribute values are considered,
allowing you to use their names for your own properties.
The deriving struct is responsible for making sure the types of fields it chooses to declare are compatible with this table.

A deriving struct is free to include or exclude any of the fields below.

[§](https://docs.rs#fromderiveinput)`FromDeriveInput`

| Field name | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ident` | `syn::Ident` | The identifier of the passed-in type |
| `vis` | `syn::Visibility` | The visibility of the passed-in type |
| `generics` | `T: darling::FromGenerics` | The generics of the passed-in type. This can be `syn::Generics`,`darling::ast::Generics`, or any compatible type. |
| `data`(or anything, using`#[darling(with = ...)]`) | `darling::ast::Data` | The body of the passed-in type |
| `attrs` | `Vec<syn::Attribute>`(or anything, using`#[darling(with = ...)]`) | The forwarded attributes from the passed in type. These are controlled using the `forward_attrs`attribute. |

[§](https://docs.rs#fromfield)`FromField`

| Field name | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ident` | `Option<syn::Ident>` | The identifier of the passed-in field, or `None`for tuple fields |
| `vis` | `syn::Visibility` | The visibility of the passed-in field |
| `ty` | `syn::Type` | The type of the passed-in field |
| `attrs` | `Vec<syn::Attribute>`(or anything, using`#[darling(with = ...)]`) | The forwarded attributes from the passed in field. These are controlled using the `forward_attrs`attribute. |

[§](https://docs.rs#fromtypeparam)`FromTypeParam`

| Field name | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ident` | `syn::Ident` | The identifier of the passed-in type param |
| `bounds` | `Vec<syn::TypeParamBound>` | The bounds applied to the type param |
| `default` | `Option<syn::Type>` | The default type of the parameter, if one exists |
| `attrs` | `Vec<syn::Attribute>`(or anything, using`#[darling(with = ...)]`) | The forwarded attributes from the passed in type param. These are controlled using the `forward_attrs`attribute. |

[§](https://docs.rs#fromvariant)`FromVariant`

| Field name | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ident` | `syn::Ident` | The identifier of the passed-in variant |
| `discriminant` | `Option<syn::Expr>` | For a variant such as `Example = 2`, the`2` |
| `fields` | `darling::ast::Fields<T> where T: FromField` | The fields associated with the variant |
| `attrs` | `Vec<syn::Attribute>`(or anything, using`#[darling(with = ...)]`) | The forwarded attributes from the passed in variant. These are controlled using the `forward_attrs`attribute. |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- Utility types for working with the AST.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- The `darling::Error`type, the multiple error`Accumulator`, and their internals.
- [usage](https://docs.rs/usage/index.html)
- Traits and types used for tracking the usage of generic parameters through a proc-macro input.
- [util](https://docs.rs/util/index.html)
- Utility types for attribute parsing.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [uses_](https://docs.rs/macro.uses_lifetimes.html)- lifetimes
- Generator for `UsesLifetimes`impls that unions the used lifetimes of the selected fields.
- [uses_](https://docs.rs/macro.uses_type_params.html)- type_ - params
- Generator for `UsesTypeParam`impls that unions the used type parameters of the selected fields.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- An error encountered during attribute parsing.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromAttributes.html)- Attributes
- Create an instance by parsing a list of attributes.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromDeriveInput.html)- Derive - Input
- Creates an instance by parsing an entire proc-macro `derive`input, including the, identity, generics, and visibility of the type.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromField.html)- Field
- Creates an instance by parsing an individual field and its attributes.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromGenericParam.html)- Generic - Param
- Creates an instance by parsing a specific `syn::GenericParam`. This can be a type param, a lifetime, or a const param.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromGenerics.html)- Generics
- Creates an instance by parsing an entire generics declaration, including the
`where`clause.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromMeta.html)- Meta
- Create an instance from an item in an attribute declaration.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromTypeParam.html)- Type - Param
- Creates an instance by parsing an individual type_param and its attributes.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromVariant.html)- Variant
- Creates an instance from a specified `syn::Variant`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)
- An alias of `Result`specific to attribute parsing.

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

# ref-cast 1.0.25 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ref-cast/1.0.25

# RefCast

Safely cast `&T` to `&U` where the struct `U` contains a single field of
type `T`.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Basic example

```
use RefCast;
;
```
Note that `#[repr(transparent)]` is required in order for the conversion to be
sound. The derive macro will refuse to compile if that is not present.

## Realistic example

Suppose we have a multidimensional array represented in a flat buffer in row-major order for performance reasons, but we want to expose an indexing operation that works in column-major order because it is more intuitive in the context of our application.

```
const MAP_WIDTH: usize = 4;
;
// `tilemap[x][y]` should give us `tilemap.storage[y * MAP_WIDTH + x]`.
```
The signature of the [ Index](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Index.html) trait in Rust is such that the output is
forced to be borrowed from the type being indexed. So something like the
following is not going to work.

```
// Does not work! The output of Index must be a reference that is
// borrowed from self. Here the type Column is not a reference.
```
Here is a working approach using `RefCast`.

```
;
// Implement `tilemap[x][y]` as `tilemap[x..][y * MAP_WIDTH]`.
```

# rustversion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustversion/^1.0.13/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]`[§](https://docs.rs#selectors)Selectors

- `#[rustversion::stable]`
 True on any stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`
 True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
- `#[rustversion::beta]`
 True on any beta compiler.
- `#[rustversion::nightly]`
 True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
- `#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`
 True on exactly one nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`
 True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
- `#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`
 True on that nightly and all newer ones.
- `#[rustversion::before(`- *version or date*- `)]`
 Negative of- *#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
- `#[rustversion::not(`- *selector*- `)]`
 Negative of any selector; for example- *#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
- `#[rustversion::any(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example- *#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
- `#[rustversion::all(`- *selectors...*- `)]`
 True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example- *#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
- `#[rustversion::attr(`- *selector*- `,`- *attribute*- `)]`
 For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to- `cfg_attr`.
- `rustversion::cfg!(`- *selector*- `)`
 An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example- *if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-cases)Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
use std::pin::Pin;
#[rustversion::since(1.33)]
impl<P: MyTrait> MyTrait for Pin<P> {
    /* ... */
}
```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
#[rustversion::attr(before(1.33), repr(packed))]
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.33), repr(packed(2)))]
struct Six(i16, i32);
fn main() {
    println!("{}", std::mem::align_of::<Six>());
}
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case
by the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[rustversion::attr(since(1.32), const)]
fn duration_as_days(dur: Duration) -> u64 {
    dur.as_secs() / 60 / 60 / 24
}
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```
// build.rs
fn main() {
    if rustversion::cfg!(since(1.36)) {
        println!("cargo:rustc-cfg=no_std");
    }
}
```
```
// src/lib.rs
#![cfg_attr(no_std, no_std)]
#[cfg(no_std)]
extern crate alloc;
```
